Synthesis:
Research on tree outplanting in elephant-inhabited areas highlights that seedling survival is primarily threatened by herbivore browsing and water stress [1][2][3]. Protective measures, such as using tree guards or fences, significantly increase sapling survival rates by excluding browsers [1][2][4]. For successful restoration, practitioners often target species tolerant of browsing or water stress, and utilize nurseries to cultivate native flora [4][3]. Elephants also naturally promote forest regeneration by dispersing seeds through their dung, which some restoration projects replicate by growing seedlings from seeds extracted from elephant waste [5][4].

To determine if tree losses have continued and gain further insights into the causes - particularly the relative importance of water stress versus debarking by elephant - tagged trees were surveyed annually from 2011 to 2022. Rates of mortality were higher than in the previous decade for four of the five dominant tree species. Bank erosion from flooding remained a cause but accounted for far less mortality than in the past. For individuals not lost to floods, survival analysis indicated that low rainfall was the primary driver of mortality. Canopy infestation by climbers did not decrease survival, and while elephant damage was common for all species and most likely killed some individuals, it had far less effect than our measures of water availability. Isotopic analysis of xylem, soil, river and groundwater revealed few differences in source water use between species, and marginal contributions from the alluvial aquifer. All species relied on deep soil water, illustrating a key linkage between rainfall and survival under the current hydrological regime. Persistence of the remaining large trees at this site is highly unlikely, considering the altered flow regime of the river and likelihood that future climate change will exacerbate water stress. Elephants By The Lake (EBTL) is a forest restoration project and learning center located in the Eastern Ghats of Tamil Nadu [1][2][3]. Supported by the Rainmatter Foundation, the 70-acre initiative focuses on regenerating degraded dry deciduous forest landscapes using permaculture principles and native flora [1][4][5]. The site also hosts workshops on ecological restoration and sustainable livelihoods [4][2]. The name is occasionally used as a title for impressionistic watercolor paintings of elephants near water [6][7] and is also an alternative name for Anayirangal Lake in Munnar, Kerala, known for its frequent elephant sightings [8].
